subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: On the leading strand during DNA replication, synthesis is:
options: Continuous, following the replication fork in a 5' to 3' direction
questions.explain: The leading strand template runs 3' to 5' towards the fork, so DNA polymerase synthesises it continuously 5' to 3'.

questions.q: ATP is resynthesised from ADP and inorganic phosphate in a reaction that is:
options: a condensation requiring energy, catalysed by ATP synthase
a spontaneous exergonic process needing no enzyme
questions.explain: Phosphorylation of ADP is an endergonic condensation reaction catalysed by ATP synthase, storing energy in the new phosphate bond.

questions.q: Collagen is a strong structural protein because:
options: it dissolves readily in water to form an enzyme
it is a globular protein with a hydrophilic exterior
it consists of a single alpha-helix
three polypeptide chains wind into a triple helix held by hydrogen bonds, with staggered cross-links between molecules
questions.explain: Collagen's three chains form a tight triple helix and adjacent molecules are covalently cross-linked in a staggered array, giving high tensile strength.

questions.q: In PCR, the function of the primers is to:
options: Cut the DNA at specific sites
Provide a starting point with a free 3'-OH for DNA polymerase
questions.explain: Primers anneal to the template and provide the free 3' end that DNA polymerase needs to begin synthesis.

questions.q: The primary structure of a protein refers to:
options: the association of multiple polypeptide subunits
the overall 3D folding stabilised by R-group interactions
the specific sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide
questions.explain: Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids determined by the gene, dictating all higher levels of folding.

questions.q: In a population, the frequency of the dominant allele (p) is 0.6. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of heterozygotes is:
The secondary structure of a protein (alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet) is stabilised primarily by:
options: hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N-H groups of the backbone
questions.explain: Secondary structure arises from regular hydrogen bonding between backbone carbonyl and amine groups, independent of R-group identity.

questions.q: A non-reducing disaccharide formed from one molecule of alpha-glucose and one of fructose is:
questions.explain: Sucrose is formed by condensation of glucose and fructose and is non-reducing because its reactive groups are involved in the glycosidic bond.

questions.q: A totipotent stem cell differs from a pluripotent stem cell because it can:
options: Differentiate into any cell type including extra-embryonic (placental) tissue
questions.explain: Totipotent cells can form all cell types of the organism plus extra-embryonic tissues, unlike pluripotent cells.

questions.q: Glycogen and amylose both store glucose, but glycogen is more highly branched. A direct consequence of this branching is that glycogen:
options: can be hydrolysed more rapidly because of more terminal glucose residues
forms straight chains that pack into fibres
questions.explain: More branch points give more free ends from which glucose can be released quickly, suiting the high metabolic rate of animals.

questions.q: In a dihybrid cross, the 9:3:3:1 ratio depends on the assumption that the two genes:
options: Assort independently (are on different chromosomes or far apart)
questions.explain: The 9:3:3:1 ratio requires independent assortment, which is only seen when genes are unlinked.

questions.q: In the Hardy-Weinberg equations, q squared represents the frequency of:
questions.explain: q squared is the frequency of the homozygous recessive genotype, since q is the recessive allele frequency.

questions.q: In a sample of double-stranded DNA, 20% of the bases are adenine. The percentage of cytosine is:
questions.explain: By Chargaff's rule A=T=20%, so G+C=60%, and since G=C, cytosine is 30%.

questions.q: In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous parents (Tt x Tt), the expected phenotypic ratio is:
questions.explain: A heterozygous monohybrid cross gives a 3:1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes.

questions.q: Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. A carrier mother and an unaffected father have children. What proportion of their sons are expected to be colour blind?
questions.explain: Sons inherit one of the mother's two X chromosomes, so half receive the affected X and are colour blind.

questions.q: DNA replication is described as semi-conservative rather than conservative because experiments showed that after one round of replication in heavy then light isotopes, all DNA was:
options: A mixture of fully heavy and fully light molecules
Of intermediate density (one heavy strand, one light strand)
questions.explain: Meselson and Stahl found a single intermediate-density band after one generation, supporting semi-conservative replication.

questions.q: How many hydrogen bonds form between guanine and cytosine in DNA?
questions.explain: Guanine and cytosine pair via three hydrogen bonds, whereas adenine and thymine pair via two.

questions.q: The genetic code is described as 'degenerate'. This means that:
options: Each codon codes for more than one amino acid
Most amino acids can be coded for by more than one codon
Some codons do not code for any amino acid
questions.explain: Degeneracy means most amino acids are specified by more than one triplet codon.

questions.q: In PCR, the temperature is raised to around 95 degrees C in order to:
options: Separate the two DNA strands by breaking hydrogen bonds
questions.explain: Denaturation at ~95 degrees C breaks the hydrogen bonds, separating the DNA into single strands.

questions.q: A substitution mutation in a coding region may have no effect on the polypeptide produced. This is most likely because:
options: The mutation occurs in an intron only
The degenerate nature of the code means the new codon may still code for the same amino acid
questions.explain: Owing to degeneracy, an altered codon can still specify the same amino acid (a synonymous/silent mutation).

questions.q: How many different codons are possible using a triplet code of four bases?
questions.explain: With four bases in groups of three, 4 cubed = 64 possible codons.

questions.q: Activated nucleotides used in DNA replication carry two extra phosphate groups. The breaking of these bonds:
options: Releases energy that drives the condensation reaction joining nucleotides
Removes errors from the new strand
questions.explain: Hydrolysis of the two additional phosphates releases energy that powers phosphodiester bond formation.

questions.q: The chi-squared test is used in genetics to:
options: Calculate allele frequencies in a population
Measure the strength of a correlation
Determine whether observed phenotypic ratios differ significantly from expected ratios
questions.explain: Chi-squared compares observed and expected categorical data to test whether differences are due to chance.

questions.q: Two genes are described as autosomally linked when they:
options: Are located close together on the same autosome and tend to be inherited together
Are located on the X chromosome
questions.explain: Linked genes lie on the same (non-sex) chromosome and tend to be inherited together rather than assorting independently.

questions.q: The biuret test detects proteins by producing a purple colour, which results from:
options: the breakdown of peptide bonds by acid
copper ions reducing to copper oxide
the formation of a complex between copper(II) ions and peptide bonds in alkaline conditions
questions.explain: In alkaline solution, copper(II) ions form a violet coordination complex with the nitrogen atoms of peptide bonds.

questions.q: In codominance, the heterozygote shows:
options: Both alleles' phenotypes fully and simultaneously
questions.explain: In codominance both alleles are expressed fully in the heterozygote, as in the AB blood group.

questions.q: Continuous variation (e.g. human height) is typically caused by:
options: A single gene with two alleles
Many genes acting together (polygenic) plus environmental influence
questions.explain: Continuous variation is polygenic, with many genes and the environment producing a range of phenotypes.

questions.q: During gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments, the fragments move towards the anode (positive electrode) because:
options: DNA carries an overall positive charge
The phosphate groups give DNA an overall negative charge
Larger fragments are repelled by the gel
questions.explain: The phosphate backbone gives DNA a net negative charge, so fragments migrate towards the positive anode.

questions.q: Oestrogen affects gene expression by:
options: Methylating cytosine bases to silence genes
Binding to DNA polymerase to speed up replication
Binding to a receptor to form a transcription factor complex that switches on target genes
questions.explain: Oestrogen binds its receptor, and the complex acts as a transcription factor that initiates transcription of target genes.

questions.q: A person with blood group AB has the genotype:
questions.explain: Group AB results from codominant alleles IA and IB both being expressed.
